Dayuan Chen Texas State University San Marcos, TX, USA dayuan@txstate.edu Ziliang Zong Texas State University San Marcos, TX, USA zz11@txstate.edu LLMs arise from the scale of the model size, dataset size, and computational resources [7, 16, 26]. Although fine-tuning provides a cost-effective alternative with strong results [8, 22], it is still computationally expensive, and its runtime, memory usage, and energy consumption can vary substantially across hardware platforms and training configurations. In practice, practitioners often use default fine-tuning hyperparameters given by the tool providers, but these settings are not necessarily optimal for a given GPU platform or fine-tuning stage. As a result, fine-tuning on the same model and dataset can exhibit very different resource utilization and energy cost depending on configuration choices.

Prior work on hyperparameter optimization has mainly focused on improving model accuracy and capability, excluding resource usage as optimization targets. Recent studies have started to connect automated tuning with sustainability, but mostly from the perspective of improving hyperparameter optimization (HPO) efficiency itself [3, 10, 14, 29]. To the best of our knowledge, resource-centric hyperparameter tuning for LLM fine-tuning has not been systematically studied.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are one of the most popular topics in the domain of Artificial Intelligence (AI). ChatGPT, an AI chat bot released in November 2022, is the fastest-growing software application in history and ranked as the 5th most visited website as of early 2026 [6, 20]. Most of these methods, such as Bayesian optimization [11] and Hyperband [18], were proposed to advance model quality, while treating runtime, memory, and energy consumption as overhead cost of running and rarely considering them as optimization objectives. Recently, several works have incorporated computational cost as one of the HPO objectives. Li et al. and Zhang et al. proposed multi-fidelity extensions of Hyperband and BOHB that adaptively allocate budget to accelerate HPO [19, 33]. Hennig et al. explored 'green AutoML' for deep shift neural networks, jointly optimizing accuracy and energy consumption [14]. In the LLM field, EcoTune focused on inference-time multi-fidelity tuning for token efficiency, and traded accuracy against token budgets [29]. In contrast, our work targets system-level objectives of LLM finetuning. To the best of our knowledge, such resource-centric HPO for LLM fine-tuning has not been studied. Optimizing model quality is complementary to our approach and can be applied in conjunction with HyperTune; therefore, we do not present model performance results in this paper.

Existing works have proposed various approaches to improve training speed and memory efficiency. Progressive layer dropping [32] speeds up transformer based model training without extra hardware resources. For memory optimization, gradient checkpointing [5] allows recomputation of activations during the backward pass, reducing memory usage to 𝑂 ( log ( 𝑛 )) with 𝑂 ( 𝑛 log ( 𝑛 )) computation overhead. Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO) [23] implements a series of memory optimization techniques by reducing data and model redundancy in training pipeline, which trade communication for memory space. Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA), one of the PEFT methods, introduced trainable rank decomposition matrices while keeping the original matrix weights unchanged, which greatly reduces the trainable parameters as well as memory use. For energy oriented optimization, GreenTrainer [15] adaptively trains a subset of tensors to achieve 64% FLOPs reduction. ELSA [13] proposed a software-hardware co-design with specialized hardware and optimized key-filtering algorithms. In our work, HyperTune is complementary to these techniques: rather than introducing new optimizers, it systematically explores existing optimization knobs to find configurations that best align with user-specified runtime, memory or energy goals during fine-tuning.

To quantify runtime, memory, and energy statistics, compare performance among different configurations, and identify potential improvements, comprehensive measurement is necessary. GPS-UP [1] proposed three metrics as greenup, powerup, and speedup to categorize software optimization efficiency. For GPU performance measurement, NVML and nvidia-smi are widely used tools for accurate measurement [9, 25]. Despite various optimizations and performance measurement techniques, finding an optimal training configuration still remains a task for end developers. Chen et al. studied that the hyperparameter space could exceed 2 36 possibilities [4], posing a significant challenge in efficiently and cost-effectively finding the best settings. You et al. [31] proposed Zeus, an optimization framework for DNN training that tunes batch size and GPU power limits, achieving significant improvements in energy efficiency. Microsoft proposed DeepSpeed library [24, 30], addresses out-of-memory, low-throughput, and slow-convergence issues in parallel training by integrating multiple optimization techniques as tunable hyperparameters. Beyond DNN training, auto-tuning frameworks such as TUNA have demonstrated that profiling-based configuration space exploration can improve the performance of cloud applications [12]. In HyperTune, we follow a similar philosophy of using profiling runs to guide configuration selection, while focusing on the system hyperparameters in LLM fine-tuning pipeline, and targeting GPU-level runtime, memory, and energy metrics as our optimization objectives.

To evaluate the optimization performance across three dimensions (runtime, memory usage, and energy consumption), and to facilitate comparison among various configurations, we utilized a simple yet effective framework consisting of three metrics: SpeedUp, MemoryUp, and EnergyUp [4].

Results presented in this paper were obtained using the Chameleon testbed [17] supported by the National Science Foundation.
